/WEDNESDAY NIGHT THROUGH MONDAY/...
Issued at 349 AM MDT Tue Oct 13 2026

Primary forecast concern will be the Pacific storm system
expected to move across the region midweek, bringing widespread
rainfall, mountain snow (down to elevations of 7500 feet, 
possibly lower but limited confidence), windy conditions, and 
much cooler temperatures.

All models show the potent mid to upper level low lifting
northeast across Colorado Wednesday night, and gradually into
southern Nebraska by Thursday. Both the ECMWF and GFS
deterministic show this general trend, with the 500mb low
tracking across northeast Colorado. The surface low is quite a
bit south, so not expecting (so far) a "slow" stacked storm
system at this time with the surface low developing across
eastern Colorado and tracking east-northeast into eastern
Nebraska by early Thursday morning. However, the NAM and
Canadian are further north with the storm system, showing it
hugging the CO/WY border with a pronounced dry slot moving into
the eastern plains Wednesday night. Due to these remaining 
uncertainties, did not increase QPF too much Wednesday night 
through Thursday, but expect a decent rainfall for most of the 
eastern plains given good upslope flow, persistent isentropic 
lift, and some jet dynamics due to an exiting 110 knot jet max. 
Precipitation and precipitation type is a little less clear 
further west, mainly along and west of the I-25 corridor. Models
have trended a bit colder, likely due to some dynamic cooling 
with this storm system. 700mb temperatures are now between -2c 
to -5c across the area. With an isothermal layer noted between 
1500 ft to 5000 ft on area soundings, this is cold enough to 
support snow, at least, down to 7000 feet...including the 
Laramie valley and the high valleys across Carbon County. 
Further east, it is very close for elevations down to 6000 feet,
including Cheyenne, where a mix rain/snow is certainly possible
Wednesday night into Thursday morning. Based on current model 
and ensemble data, intermittent change over(s) to snow and 
rain/snow mix are expected between 6500 to 7500 feet where some 
light accumulation possible on grassy and elevated surfaces. 
However, most of these valleys (west of the Laramie Range) will 
struggle with some easterly downslope flow off the Laramie Range 
as winds start to increase and shift east and southeast. This 
is why POP is a bit lower for Laramie, Saratoga, and Rawlins. 
High confidence that the mountains will receive accumulating 
snowfall with Winter Weather Advisory conditions expected 
Wednesday through Thursday. May need to issue these shortly, but
we have additional time to fine tune the accumulation details. 
The bigger question is the Arlington/Elk Mountain are and the 
I-80 Summit between Laramie and Cheyenne. Currently, snowlevels 
are low enough to warrant Winter Weather Advisory amounts. 
However, not very confident on QPF amounts in this area and if 
any snow will stick to the roadways. Will continue to monitor 
this potential with future updates.

Otherwise, models have trended a bit stronger on winds late 
Wednesday night and Thursday with a stronger pressure gradient 
behind the surface low and 700mb winds increasing out of the 
north between 40 to 50 knots. North winds gusting up to 45 MPH 
possible through Thursday afternoon across the eastern plains.

Precipitation will diminish from west to east Thursday into 
early Friday morning with clearing skies. This is our most
favorable period to see frost and a hard freeze. Currently,
forecast low temperatures are in the 20s to near the upper teens
across south central Wyoming, including the Laramie Valley. Mid
20s to low 30s forecast for the eastern plains. This is 
generally around the 25th to 50th percentile of the NBM and the
12z Grand Ensemble which seems to fit this general pattern as 
some colder air sneaks around the backside of the storm system 
Thursday night. Would like to note that the new 00z Grand is
even colder with 25th percentile lows around the mid teens to
low 20s. Freeze and/or Frost headlines expected, but will wait 
until this storm is through the area first. Friday will be 
seasonably cool under northwest flow aloft with highs in the 50s
to low 60s.

Medium to Long Range models appear to be in reasonable agreement
for next weekend, showing a broad ridge axis translating
eastward into the Front Range from the eastern Pacific. Expect
drier weather with pleasant daytime temperatures for mid October
with highs in the 60s to low 70s...and some mid 70s for western
Nebraska. Low temperatures will be seasonable and generally in
the 30s to low 40s into next Monday morning.
